claim: President Donald Trump's 2018 budget proposal calls for cuts in benefits to highly disabled veterans
label: half
explain: As a presidential candidate, one of Donald Trump’s main campaign promises was to improve the treatment of United States military veterans and initiate major reforms to the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA).However, the president faced criticism during 2018 budget talks amidst reports that he was proposing significant cuts to benefits for disabled veterans. On 17 January 2018, a meme appeared on social media that specified a facet of that criticism:As is usually the case with memes and macros, this was not an entirely accurate summation of the political situation. President Trump did propose cutting a particular benefit for some disabled veterans in his March 2017 federal budget proposal; however, his administration backed away from the plan after an outcry from veterans’ groups and abandoned the provisions that would have produced those cuts.The Facebook meme appeared to have originated in an analysis of President Trump’s budget plan contained in journalist David Cay Johnston’s book . On page 225, Johnston wrote that:The benefit  is called “individual unemployability” (IU) and is paid out (as part of the Department of Veterans Affairs disability compensation program) to military veterans who are unable to find work because they have a relatively high level of disability sustained during service in the armed forces,  according to the VA:In order to qualify for IU, a veteran must be assessed as being at least 60 percent disabled due to a service-connected disability or disabilities.As Johnston correctly wrote, Donald Trump’s initial 2018 budget proposal ended individual unemployability for disabled veterans once they became eligible to receive Social Security benefits. However, Johnston did not mention that, under President Trump’s proposal, disabled veterans who received Social Security benefits would continue to be paid disability benefits by the VA, albeit at their originally-assessed disability rate (rather than at a 100 percent rate), and anyone not eligible for Social Security would continue to receive IU.The 2018 budget proposal outlined the proposed changes:The Trump administration estimated that the proposed cuts would save $3.2 billion in 2018 and $40.8 billion over 10 years and had proposed using those savings to help fund a plan to expand and make permanent the Obama administration’s Veterans Choice Program, which seeks to improve the availability of care for veterans in their own communities. Veterans organizations strongly criticized the IU proposal in early 2017, with veterans service organization AMVETS warning that it was “deeply concerned” by the cuts, which they said would affect “perhaps the most vulnerable segment of the veterans population”:AMVETS estimated that Trump’s proposal would affect 225,000 military veterans aged over 65 and would decrease by a full $1,200 a month the disability benefit paid to an unmarried veteran with a 90 percent disabled rating. The payments that veterans receive under IU depends upon their disability rating and family circumstances, as outlined by the VA. For example, a veteran with a 60 percent disability rating who lives alone would theoretically receive $1,083.52 in disability benefits each month. However, under individual unemployability, veterans are treated as if they had a disability rating of 100 percent, meaning they would receive $2,973.86 each month.  For veterans eligible to receive Social Security, Trump’s plan would have pruned their monthly disability benefit back to the 60 percent rate, a highly significant cut of $1,890.34, or 63.6 percent. Over the course of a year, that would have brought their disability benefits down from $35,686.32 to $13,002.24, roughly the amounts mentioned by David Cay Johnston in his book and in the Facebook meme.Such veterans would be in receipt of Social Security benefits as well, but it’s easy to see the significant financial effects the plan would have had on an aging veteran who was unable to work and who lived alone.By comparison, a retirement-aged veteran with a 90 percent disability rating and a dependent spouse, a child, and two parents would have seen annual disability benefits cut from $42,326.64 to $27,356.16, a decrease of 35.4 percent.In June 2017, VA Secretary David Shulkin publicly stepped back from the proposed IU cut, telling the Senate Veterans’ Affair Committee that:The following October, Shulkin wrote to veterans service organizations to confirm that the VA no longer supported ending IU for disabled veterans who are eligible to receive Social Security.Johnston’s analysis, and the Facebook meme posted by Stacey Sharp, are both true in a narrow sense. The amounts they mentioned were accurate but were based on only one of many possible scenarios for disabled veterans.  The latter, published in January 2018, left out that the proposal had been abandoned by then.

Despite vow to support America ’ s veteran , President Donald Trump and congressional Republican leader have put forth budget proposal that be poise to do great damage to the economic security of veteran and their families—all to pay for tax cut for millionaire and corporations.1 In fact , for every $ 2 of the cut Trump want to make to service and benefit for veteran , which will total more than $ 154 billion over the next decade , Trump plan to give more than $ 3 to the adult child of millionaire and billionaire . The potential toll of these destructive action spearhead by the Trump administration not only reveal Trump ’ s deceitful betrayal of veteran but also eviscerate his claim that he be improve veteran ’ access to timely , quality care.25
President Trump ’ s propose $ 72 billion in deep cut to the nation ’ s disability support over the next decade would also be disastrous for veterans.26 Nearly 1 million veteran receive Social Security Disability Insurance benefit in 2013,27 but President Trump want to add more red tape that would make it hard for people with disability to access the benefit they have earned.28 Cuts to Social Security would be on top of President Trump ’ s budget proposal to eliminate the Individual Unemployability benefit program , which permit the VA to provide benefit at the 100 percent-disabled rate to veteran who be unable to get a job because of service-connected disability , even if their disability be not rat at the 100 percent level.29
This propose elimination—which be put on hold in response to fierce opposition from veteran groups—would cut disability benefit for old veteran , include more than 225,000 veteran currently receive benefits.30 Additionally , President Trump have propose eliminate the Limb Loss Resource Center and the Paralysis Resource Center,31 both of which provide essential support for veteran , who be disproportionately likely to be paralyze and have elevate rate of traumatic amputation.32
Veterans and their family make up a sizeable share of Americans face food insecurity.33 In a recent long-term study of veteran , nearly 1 in 4 participant experience food insecurity and be more likely to have difficulty stay healthy a a result . The propose cut to the Public Housing Capital Fund—the main source of federal funding for the preservation of public housing—could mean that many struggle veteran reside in distressed public housing unit would continue to live in unsafe dwellings.50 Further , by slash funding for the CDBG program and the National Housing Trust Fund , the propose budget would significantly curtail local anti-homelessness effort to develop and provide affordable housing and supportive service for veterans.51
The Trump agenda also call for the elimination of the Legal Services Corporation ( LSC ) , which provide low-income individual with civil legal aid to reconnect them with vital benefit and service that , among many thing , can help them stay in their home , fight discriminatory business practice , and escape abusive environments.52 More than 1.7 million veteran be income-eligible for LSC services.53 Last year alone , LSC-funded organization work on roughly 41,000 civil legal case involve household that include veteran struggle to make end meet.54 The civil legal problem that many of these vulnerable veteran face often relate to their discharge status , barrier to care for service-related health issue , and deny service benefits.55
Both veteran and their family have make sacrifice for this country . Previous congressional Republican attempt to repeal and replace the Affordable Care Act ( ACA ) would have cost close to half a million veteran their Medicaid benefit by 2026.5 And the most recent repeal effort , which make devastate change to Medicaid,6 would be even bad , cost an estimate 579,000 veteran their Medicaid coverage within a decade.7
This analysis largely focus on President Trump ’ s budget since the budget put forth by congressional leader include few detail , make it impossible to know in many instance exactly how it would harm veteran . Additionally , CAP estimate that over the next decade , 400,000 veteran on average could lose access to critical nutrition assistance each year if the cut propose in President Trump ’ s budget be apply directly to participation in the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program ( SNAP ) . If implement through a reduction in the number of people participate in the program , the cut of nearly $ 200 billion that Trump propose for SNAP over the next decade could snatch critical nutrition assistance away from an average of 400,000 veteran per year—needlessly expose them to the threat of hunger and malnourishment.35
The House budget deliver an almost equally devastate blow to SNAP , cut $ 154 billion over 10 years.36 But since the House majority budget concentrate it cut in the final year of the budget window—slashing project SNAP spending by 42 percent between 2023 and 2027—its plan could result in an even great number of veteran lose access in those year : All tell , more than 554,000 veteran could lose SNAP coverage each year between 2023 and 2027.37
Nearly two-thirds of the people report a homeless or living in shelter in the 2016 single-night census conduct by the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development ( HUD ) be veterans.38 Rental assistance be critical in help veteran afford decent housing and in prevent and reduce veteran homelessness . The public workforce system , authorize by the Workforce Innovation and Opportunity Act ( WIOA ) , serve nearly 1 million veteran each year , offer service such a career development , job training , and job search assistance.10 Yet the Trump administration ’ s propose budget cut would result in thousand of veteran lose access to these program and service . In 2015 , for example , the WIOA adult , dislocate worker , and youth program serve more than 80,000 veterans.11 The Trump budget would cut funding for these service by 43 percent from 2015 level , mean that more than 34,000 veteran could lose access to essential services.12 The Trump budget would also cut the Wagner-Peyser Employment Service by 36 percent from 2015 levels.13 This service provide labor-exchange service to jobseekers , include 858,000 veteran . The Section 811 program , however , would be downsize under Trump ’ s budget proposal.49 The propose budget would also affect veteran who reside in public housing unit in need of major repair . Nearly one-third of federal employee hire in 2015 be veteran , and close to half of these be veteran with disabilities.8
Now , despite promise to invest more9 in training opportunity for veteran , the Trump budget would make it more difficult for veteran to access essential job training and employment service . Despite the common belief to the contrary , veteran-specific benefit and service fall short of meet the need of veteran and their family , many of whom struggle to meet basic need even with Department of Veterans Affairs ( VA ) supports.3 More than 3.9 million veteran live paycheck to paycheck—meaning their family income be less than twice the federal poverty level , or less than $ 50,000 for a family of four.4 Yet new CAP analysis reveals that if Trump ’ s propose cut to key job train program be apply directly to program participation , more than 340,000 veteran could lose access to critical employment service that help boost wage . If instead the cut propose in the House of Representatives Republican budget be apply , more than 554,000 veteran could lose SNAP each year between 2023 and 2027 .

Like his previous budget , the President ’ s 2020 budget call for make the 2017 tax cut permanent while make deep cut to entitlement program that help low- and moderate-income family afford the basic and provide them with access to health care . The budget ’ s major theme be perhaps nowhere clear than in it proposal to extend beyond 2025 the costly 2017 tax cut that have give large windfall to high-income individual and highly profitable corporation — even a the budget call for cut $ 1 trillion over the next decade from entitlement ( mandatory ) program that help low- and moderate-income household . The President ’ s 2020 budget call for deep cut in housing program . The Trump proposal would cut that payment in half . The Trump Administration ’ s budget plan for fiscal year 2020 mirror last year ’ s in the massive cut it propose for core public service that help struggle individual and family afford the basic and access health care . Expanding on the Trump Administration ’ s unprecedented approval of state work requirement policy in Medicaid , the President ’ s budget propose to take coverage away from adult nationwide if they don ’ t meet a work requirement . One Administration budget proposal would cut in half the retroactive benefit that disable worker may receive .
